prompt: Let $h(x) = \int_0^{x^2} \cos t \, dt$. Which expression equals $h'(x)$?
hint: The upper limit is $x^2$, not $x$. That makes $h$ a composition: $h(x) = G(x^2)$ where $G(u) = \int_0^u \cos t \, dt$. Chain rule!

hints.title: 🪜 Try a simpler one
hints.text: Warm up: if $G(u) = \int_0^u \cos t \, dt$, then by the FTC $G'(u) = \cos u$. Now $h(x) = G(x^2)$, so $h'(x) = G'(x^2) \cdot (x^2)'$.

explanation: Write $h(x) = G(u)$ with $u = x^2$ and $G(u) = \int_0^u \cos t \, dt$. By the FTC, $G'(u) = \cos u$.
Choice A. Choice B forgets the chain rule factor; C and D confuse "derivative of the integral" with actually integrating $\cos$ to get $\sin$.

alternativeExplanations.title: Integrate first, then differentiate
steps: Same answer. This route works here because $\cos$ has a simple antiderivative; the FTC-plus-chain-rule route works even when it does not.
